title: THE WORKSHOP OF MAGOS YTTRIX CAEL
revisit: Oil and tea. A bench, a kettle, a Magos who is pleased to see you, and an Enginseer-Adjunct who is pleased about telemetry.
intro:
Warm. Tidy. It smells of oil and tea, in that order, and the tea is real.

Magos Yttrix Cael has served the Adamant Crown for sixty years and maintains
every cogitator in it, including the one that was Vosk's and is now yours. He
is not frightening. That is the first thing you notice about him and it goes
on being the thing you notice.

Enginseer-Adjunct Orven Tass is at the bench behind him, twenty-six, delighted
by everything, entirely without discretion.

On the bench, half-built, under a cloth that Cael does not trouble to move, is
a harness.

"Ah," says Cael. "Yes. I thought you might come about the savant."

You have not said anything about the savant.

The work-docket pinned beside it is dated three weeks ago.
look:
A workshop that is warm and smells of tea, which no workshop in this hive is.

The BENCH, and on it a half-built mnemonic SHROUD under a cloth.
The DOCKET pinned beside it, dated three weeks ago.
A KETTLE, and two cups, and a third that has been got out.

MAGOS CAEL. Enginseer-Adjunct TASS behind him, radiating helpfulness.

objects.careless: A harness, half-built, on a bench under a cloth Cael does not trouble to move. Sixty years of work in this room and it is the only thing on the bench.
objects.careful:
A mnemonic shroud: a field-former sized for a human skull, a seating harness, and a governor calibrated in units you do not recognise.

It is beautiful work and it is two-thirds finished and it has been two-thirds finished for three weeks.

There is exactly one man in the Thessaline sector with a mnemonic augmetic worth shrouding, and until eight days ago nobody in this hive had any reason at all to think he needed it.

objects.careless: The work-docket, pinned to the bench beside the harness. Dated three weeks ago. Signed by Cael, unrequested, unbilled.
objects.careful:
Three weeks, four days.

Eleven weeks ago Hadrian Vosk opened four case-files and left them open. Three weeks ago Magos Yttrix Cael began building a shroud for a savant nobody had asked him to protect. Eight days ago you started this investigation.

The docket has a field for the originating request. It is empty. He has written, in the margin, in a very neat hand: *anticipated*.

objects.careless: A kettle, and two cups, and a third cup that has been got out and not yet filled.
objects.careful:
The third cup is for you and it was got out before you knocked.

You have not eaten in a day and a half and you are going to drink the tea, and it is going to be good, and you are going to notice about four hours later that you agreed to something while you were drinking it.

objects.careless: Enginseer-Adjunct Orven Tass, twenty-six, at the bench behind Cael, visibly hoping to be asked something.
objects.careful:
He will tell you anything. Not indiscreetly — he has no concept of discretion, because nothing he does has ever needed any, and he has been given a genuinely interesting problem by a man he admires.

If you want to know what the shroud does, ask Cael. If you want to know what it *sends*, ask Tass, and he will tell you at length, fondly, and be pleased you were interested.

npcs.title: Magos Yttrix Cael
npcs.topic_refusal: "Ask," says Cael. "I have never once been asked enough questions in this room."
npcs.portrait: Magos Yttrix Cael. Sixty years maintaining every cogitator in the Adamant Crown, including the one that was Vosk's. Warm, unhurried, entirely unfrightening, which is the thing you keep noticing.
npcs.greeting:
He pours the tea before you have asked for it, which is how he does most things.

"The savant," Cael says. "Aleth Fenn. Mnemonic augmetic, Hexta-pattern, fitted at nineteen — I did the last two services myself, he is very easy to work on because he is interested.

"You will have noticed something. I would rather you told me than that I guessed, so that I know which of us is wrong."
npcs.reprise: He waits, with the kettle, entirely unhurried.
npcs.unknown: "I don't know," Cael says, comfortably. "I could find out."
deflect: He considers it for slightly too long, and then pours more tea.

topics.text:
"Burned parchment." Cael puts the kettle down, which he does not do. "How burned?"

"Completely. It went into a censer and I have the censer."

"Then it's carbon on carbon and it is *absolutely* recoverable, and I would like you to know that I have wanted somebody to bring me this problem for about nine years."

He is already moving. The imager is a Mechanicus spectral bench that reads differential across the burn — ink carbon and parchment carbon do not oxidise at the same rate, and the ink remembers being ink for a surprisingly long time.

"Four passes. Tuesday, if the tier-four cogitators behave, which they will because I am the reason they behave."

He does not ask what it is. It does not occur to him to ask what it is; you have brought him a *technical problem*, on a Tuesday, and he is delighted, and this is a favour freely given and there is no ledger anywhere that it goes on.

"There's a censer," you say, and stop, because you are not certain there is.

There is. Sergeant Oduya took it off the Provost's inventory on the first
morning, before the wardens had finished with the corridor, and has had it in
a crate under a bench on tier one for eleven weeks.

"Course I did, sir," she says later, mildly offended by the question. "He
taught me that. Anything burned in a room, you take the ash and you don't ask
why till after. Twenty-six years, and it's come up twice, and the first time
was him teaching me."

Cael puts the kettle down, which he does not do.

"Carbon on carbon," he says. "Absolutely recoverable. Four passes. I would
like you to know I have wanted somebody to bring me this problem for about
nine years."

He does not ask what it is. You have brought him a *technical problem*, on a
Tuesday, and he is delighted, and this is a favour freely given and there is
no ledger anywhere that it goes on.

"Older than the ink," Cael says. "Older than the *idea* of the ink. I put it
against four reference corpora and got nothing to three decimal places, which
is rare enough that I enjoyed it."

He pours.

"Vosk collected things like that. A mind for dead scripts — he'd bring me a
rubbing off a lintel once a year and we'd not get anywhere with it and he'd be
perfectly happy. I always thought it was a waste in a man who could have done
real work."

He is being fond about the thing that stopped his friend's heart, in the room
where he developed it, holding a cup of tea.

"Do you know what it says?"

"No," you say.

"A mnemonic shroud. It formers a null field around the augmetic — not around the man, the augmetic; he'll feel nothing and it doesn't touch him." He turns it so you can see the seating. "The Hexta lattice is a retrieval index. It doesn't store, it *finds*, and finding is an operation, and an operation can be interfered with by a sufficiently loud environment.

"Cantor is a very loud environment. Eleven hundred relays, four hundred years of repeaters, coverage from the Spire to the sump."

He says all of it honestly and exhaustively and without one word of evasion.

"It will not undo anything. I want to be exact about that, because you are going to want me to have said something else. It reduces the rate. About a third, on the bench; I would want to measure it on him."

"Because a savant is expensive and Cantor is loud."

It is true. You can hear that it is true. It is also, for a man who has just explained a null-field former in four hundred words without being asked twice, remarkably short.

"Three weeks, Magos."

"Yes."

"Nobody asked you."

"No." He pours. "It seemed to me that it would be wanted."

You press him a third time and he does not become evasive, which is the part you will think about later. He becomes *puzzled* — a man patting his pockets for a reason he is entirely certain he had when he came out.

"I'm sorry, Inquisitor. I built it because it wanted building. I have been doing this for sixty years and that is not usually a sentence I have to defend."

[ CAEL_SUSPECTED ]

"It wants recalibrating every eleven hours or the field wanders." He turns the harness so you can see the seating. "Tass will handle it. He'll want a telemetry line — nothing exotic. Position and field-strength, twenty bytes a burst."

Position.

Behind him Tass, delighted to be relevant, supplies the rest before anybody asks him for it: burst interval, packet shape, the repeater chain it rides, and — fondly, at length, as a point of professional pride — the fact that it terminates at the workshop bench, because where else would calibration data go.

"It's very small," Cael says.

He is right. He pours the tea before you can answer, and it is good tea, and you have not eaten in a day and a half.

[ B3 HELD ]

"I maintained his machine for three years and I never once had to." Cael is briefly, genuinely warm. "Cael-pattern, three years old, and in three years he brought it in twice, both times to have the auto-quill drum cleaned, which he could have done himself and which I think he liked an excuse for.

"He asked me a question in the spring that I have thought about since." He sets the cup down. "He asked me whether a cogitator can be made to forget that it has forgotten something. I said no, of course, because a machine keeps a write-log and a write-log is not the thing it writes about.

"He said: *and if the log is the thing that was written?*

"I told him that was theology and not engineering, and he laughed, and he took his drum and went."

"Your query tier is wrong," Cael says, as though mentioning a loose button. "You were elevated into a rosette but the Vault is still indexing you at your predecessor's clerk grade, because the Crown updates authority and the Lexicanum updates *tier* and the two offices do not speak.

"You have been running third-tier queries for eight days and wondering why the Vault is slow with you."

He fixes it while he is talking, on his own terminal, in about forty seconds, unasked.

"There. Second tier. You'll get aisle-level returns and the clerks will stop making you wait."

It is genuinely useful, it is freely given, and there is now one more thing in this hive that knows what you are looking for before you look for it.

[ QUERY_TIER +1 ]

beats.text:
"Before we do," Cael says, without any change of tone at all, "the shroud."

You wait.

"It has not sent me a burst since the day you took it. Eleven weeks of nothing
from an instrument that reports every eleven hours, and I have not raised it,
and I would like you to say it out loud rather than let me go on pretending I
haven't noticed, because the pretending is undignified for both of us."

So you say it. You cut the telemetry line before you let him fit it.

"Thank you." He is not angry, which is worse. "I built that line because I did
not know what was happening to him and I wanted to be able to see it, and you
cut it because you did not know what was happening in this building and you
wanted nobody to be able to see *you*, and we were both right, and it has cost
us a fortnight of not trusting each other.

"That's the price. Say it and it's said. Now bring me the ash."

shows.text:
You tell him: twice, in the same words at the same syllable, in a room with two metres of rockcrete and no plate in it.

Cael puts the cup down and does not pick it up again for some time.

"Then it is not proximity," he says.

"No."

"Then my shroud is a bandage." He says it without any self-pity at all, as a finding. "It will slow the rate of a process I have just been told does not require the thing I designed it to exclude. I will give it to you anyway, because a third is a third and I have nothing better, and because I would like you to come back and tell me what it turns out to be.

"Inquisitor — I would be grateful if you did not tell the Adjunct that."

acts.refused: There is nothing on the bench you have been offered yet.
acts.text:
You accept it.

Tass fits it in forty minutes, talking the whole time, and Fenn is fascinated and asks better questions than you do. The seating sits under the dressing behind his ear and is not visible under a collar.

It works. It will go on working. Drift at a third the rate is the difference between a savant you can take into the hive and a savant you can visit.

The telemetry line goes live at the same moment, because it is part of the calibration and nobody in this room has suggested otherwise, and it sends position and field-strength every eleven hours to a bench in a warm room that smells of tea.

Magos Yttrix Cael has given you, freely and at his own cost, the most useful object anybody will hand you in this act.

[ FENN_SHIELDED ]

acts.refused: There is no line to cut.
acts.text:
You have the line cut.

Not refused — cut, afterwards, quietly, by an Arbites tech on tier two who does not ask why and bills you eleven crowns. The harness recalibrates off an internal governor and drifts about four per cent worse and Fenn does not notice.

Cael never mentions it.

He must know within the day; a line that stops is a line that stops. He never raises it, never asks, never adjusts his manner by so much as a degree, and goes on pouring the tea.

You are going to think about that silence for the rest of this investigation, and in Act III you will still not know whether it was courtesy, or complicity, or a man who could not remember why the line had mattered.

[ CAEL_DECEIVED ]

You decline it.

Cael is not offended and does not press. He puts the cloth back over the harness and pours you more tea and asks after the Sergeant's shoulder.

Aleth Fenn stays in a box on sub-level four, or he comes out into eleven hundred metres of coverage without a bandage on.

Nothing in this hive now knows where he is except you.

[ CAEL_REFUSED ]

It resolves in four passes.

He watches three of them with you. The first is nothing, the second is a
smear, and the third comes up far enough to show that there is a hand on it at
all, and he spends most of that pass talking about the ink — an iron-gall with
a binder he does not recognise, decanted from something older, which pleases
him enormously and which he mentions twice.

During the fourth he goes out to put the kettle on, because the fourth takes
nineteen minutes and he has been up since the fifth hour with the tier-four
cogitators.

The fourth pass is the Erratum.

Twenty-one glyphs, in a hand that predates every alphabet you have a name for,
lying on a plate on a bench in a workshop that smells of tea. You look at it
for slightly under a second before you understand that you should not be
looking at it, and by then you have looked at it.

Cael comes back in with two cups and glances at the plate on his way past the
bench.

Tass glances at it while he is racking the others.

Neither of them reads pre-Imperial. Neither of them looks at it for more than
a second and neither of them ever will, and both of them are going to be alive
next week because of that and neither of them is ever going to know it.

He puts it in a felt case and hands it to you.

"Mind the edges," he says. "They'll take a finger off and you won't feel it
till after."

He has been reconciled. There is a hole in him eleven weeks wide and it is
exactly the shape of the object he has just put into your hands, and he is
smiling at you over a cup of tea.

There is no cogitator representation of the thing you are now carrying. It is
a plate. The archive does not know it exists.

[ B21 HELD ]
[ B22 HELD ]

You tell him what he has been holding.

Not all of it. Enough: that the man who brought him rubbings off lintels for
three years died four minutes after writing twenty-one glyphs and burning
them, that the glyphs are the reason, and that Cael and his apprentice have
both had it on a bench in front of them and are both alive because neither of
them can read.

Magos Yttrix Cael goes grey. It is a specific and physical thing and you watch
it happen over about four seconds.

"Tass is nineteen," he says.

"I know."

"Tass is *nineteen*, and he racks the plates, and he has been racking that
plate for eleven days, and if he had a talent for old scripts instead of a
talent for bearings I would have had to write to his mother."

He puts the cup down without drinking any of it.

"I would like you to go, please. I am not angry with you and I would like you
to go, and I would like the plate to go with you, and I would like you to not
bring me the next one."

You go.

It is the first time in this investigation that somebody has been afraid of
you and been right to be.

exits.text: Out into the corridor, where it is cold and smells of nothing.

B3.label: The shroud sends position and field-strength every eleven hours, to Cael's bench — and he built it three weeks before anybody asked
B3.file_text:
FILED. CLASS: EQUIPMENT / MECHANICUS LIAISON. INDEXED.

ENTRY READS: MNEMONIC SHROUD, CAEL-PATTERN, ISSUED TO RETINUE SAVANT.
             CALIBRATION TELEMETRY ACTIVE. NO ACTION REQUIRED.

It is a correct and complete description of a piece of equipment, filed in an archive, where the Magos who issued it maintains the cogitator that holds the archive.
B3.note_text:
You write down two things and put a line between them.

One: the telemetry sends position, every eleven hours, to a bench.

Two: the docket is dated three weeks ago and the originating-request field is empty and he has written *anticipated* in the margin.

You do not know what the line between them means. You write the line anyway.

B21.label: THE ERRATUM — an imaging plate, twenty-one glyphs, in a hand older than the idea of the ink
B21.refusal:
You have the plate in one hand and your own pen in the other, and there is a
field on the form for RECOVERED MATERIAL, and it is the correct field.

You put the pen down.

You do not write down why.

B22.label: Cael's imaging log — four passes, nineteen minutes, his own signature on the recovery, and no idea what he recovered
B22.file_text:
FILED. CLASS: TECHNICAL / MATERIAL RECOVERY. INDEXED. ATTRIBUTED: YTTRIX CAEL, MAGOS.

A clean filing. Four passes, nineteen minutes on the fourth, an iron-gall ink
with an unidentified binder, and a Magos's signature under it.

It establishes beyond argument that Yttrix Cael handled the object, and it
says nothing whatever about what the object is, because he did not know and
the form has no field for what a man did not know.

Somebody two tiers up is going to find that useful.
B22.note_text:
His bench log, copied out: four passes, the third a smear, the fourth
nineteen minutes, an iron-gall with a binder he could not place.

His signature at the bottom, because he signs everything, because he is a
Magos of the Adeptus Mechanicus and a tidy man.

It proves he had it. It proves he did not know. Those are two different
sentences and by Act III somebody is going to want only the first one.

strings.no_such_thing: Nothing here by that name, and everything in this room is where Cael put it.
strings.already_read: You have looked twice. The tea is going cold.
strings.no_terminal: There is a terminal here and it is the Magos's, and requisitioning the Lexicanum Vault from the machine of the man who maintains the Lexicanum Vault is a thing you could do.
